idiom_name: mutable.LinkedHashMap for local LRU; concurrent.TrieMap for shared; Caffeine via JVM interop
implementation_notes: Scala's collections already pair hashing with ordering: mutable.LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order and exposes its head as the oldest entry, so the LRU policy is remove-the-head-at-capacity plus re-insert-on-hit - the doubly linked list of the classic structure disappears into the library. Shared caches use scala.collection.concurrent.TrieMap (lock-free reads, high write concurrency) with an explicit eviction sweep, and pure memoization is expressed with a private Map or a memoized function. On the JVM, production Scala code normally binds Caffeine (or Guava) for TTL, weighing and statistics; Scala's own collections win when the cache is small, local and dependency-free.
pitfalls: mutable.LinkedHashMap is not thread-safe; TrieMap is, but has no ordering, so an LRU policy needs a separate recency structure or a library cache.
LinkedHashMap order is insertion order, so a hit must remove and re-insert the key - get() becomes a write and there is no lock-free read path.
Memoizing with an immutable Map (var m = Map.empty; m += k -> v) copies the map on every insertion: fine for a handful of entries, quadratic for large caches.
Scala 2.13/3 collections differ in default mutability and conversion APIs; a cache written against one may silently copy on the other.
